6.1
The Collapse of the League · Section 6.1

The decline of international cooperation in the 1930s

The Great Depression transformed economic hardship into political and international insecurity. It weakened both the will and the means to maintain collective security.

The Wall Street Crash, 1929

Banks and businesses failed in the USA. American loans and purchases shrank, spreading unemployment and economic depression internationally.

Extremism and insecurity

Desperate voters turned towards parties promising jobs, national revival and decisive leadership. In Germany, the Nazis exploited economic desperation, resentment and antisemitic scapegoating.

Expansionism

Hitler and Mussolini promised national prestige, territory and resources; invading neighbours seemed an attractive diversion from domestic problems.

The League loses support

Countries facing unemployment wanted to protect trade and avoid the cost of war. Economic sanctions were less attractive because they could damage their own economies.

Cause → consequence: US crash → international depression → unemployment and political extremism → aggressive foreign policy → weaker support for League sanctions.

Source B · 1934 German railway worker

The worker described closed factories, hunger and his decision to join the Nazi Party in 1930. The account is useful for understanding one personal response, but cannot represent every unemployed German.

GCSE tip: connect source content to the wider Depression, and discuss perspective and limitations rather than claiming every German supported Hitler.

6.2
The Collapse of the League · Section 6.2

The Manchurian Crisis

Manchuria, in north-east China, became the centre of Japan’s expansion because of its resources, railways and strategic position.

Economic motives

Japan relied heavily on exports, especially silk. The Depression reduced demand. Manchuria offered coal, iron, farmland and markets.

Strategic foothold

Japan already had interests in the South Manchurian Railway and the Kwantung Army in the region. This made rapid military action easier.

Weak Chinese control

China was politically divided; local warlords exercised power in several regions. Japanese commanders considered this an opportunity.

Army independence and prestige

Japanese military officers increasingly acted without civilian government authorisation. Military pride and resentment after naval limitations fed expansionist ideas.

Select a date to reveal what happened and why it mattered.
Important distinction: The Japanese military claimed that Chinese soldiers attacked the railway. Historians generally regard the Mukden Incident as a pretext engineered by Japanese officers; do not present the Japanese accusation as established fact.

6.3
The Collapse of the League · Section 6.3

How did the League react to the Manchurian Crisis?

The League condemned aggression but failed to reverse it. Its slow investigation and reluctance to enforce sanctions exposed fundamental limits of collective security.

Why so little urgency?

Manchuria was far from Geneva. Britain and France were dealing with the Depression and feared conflict in East Asia.

Why were sanctions difficult?

Japan traded with the USA, which was outside the League; the USSR was also not a member. An embargo risked economic costs without guaranteeing success.

The Lytton Commission

Lord Lytton led an investigation, and the report published in October 1932 criticised Japan’s occupation. The inquiry took many months.

Consequences

Japan rejected the findings and left the League in 1933. Britain and France did not send an army. Other aggressors saw that League condemnation might not lead to action.

Grade 9 judgement: Manchuria damaged the League’s authority, but some contemporaries still thought it might protect peace in Europe. Its failure was not yet universally seen as fatal.

6.4
The Collapse of the League · Section 6.4

Why did Italy invade Abyssinia?

In 1935 Mussolini attacked Abyssinia (modern Ethiopia), one of the few independent African countries, seeking empire, resources and prestige.

Build a “new Roman Empire”

Mussolini promised national glory and overseas expansion. Controlling Abyssinia would connect or extend Italian possessions in Eritrea and Somaliland.

Revenge for Adwa, 1896

Italy’s defeat by Abyssinia was remembered as national humiliation; victory could restore prestige.

Domestic pressure

The Depression caused unemployment and dissatisfaction. Overseas military success offered a rallying cause.

Why he expected little opposition

The League’s weakness at Corfu and in Manchuria encouraged Mussolini. Britain and France wanted Italy as a partner against Hitler, especially after the Stresa discussions.

Interactive timeline · choose a date

Select a date to reveal what happened and why it mattered.
Wal Wal to war: The border clash of December 1934 became a pretext. Italy invaded in October 1935; Addis Ababa fell in May 1936. Abyssinian soldiers resisted but were outgunned, and Italian forces used chemical weapons.

6.5
The Collapse of the League · Section 6.5

How did the League respond to the Abyssinian Crisis?

Unlike Manchuria, this crisis was in a region of direct European concern. The League still could not protect its member state.

Economic sanctions — incomplete

League members restricted some trade and arms supplies with Italy. Oil, coal and iron were not effectively blocked, so the measures did not stop the invasion.

The Suez Canal stayed open

Britain and France could have impeded supply routes through Suez, but feared pushing Italy into Germany’s camp.

The Hoare–Laval plan

In December 1935 British and French ministers secretly discussed giving Italy substantial Abyssinian territory. When it leaked, public outrage followed.

Wider outcome

The League appeared to serve the interests of great powers rather than collective security. Abyssinia was conquered, and Italy later abandoned the League.

League said / plannedWhat actually happenedConsequence
Collective securityMajor powers prioritised Italy as an allyConfidence in the Covenant fell
Economic sanctionsKey fuels remained availableItalian troops could continue fighting
Protect membersAbyssinia lost its capital in May 1936League credibility suffered a devastating blow
Source B · Anthony Eden, June 1936: Eden argued that without universal membership, oil restrictions could not succeed through League action alone. Evaluate this as an explanation by a British foreign secretary defending policy.

6.6
The Collapse of the League · Section 6.6

Was the League of Nations destined to fail?

There was no single cause. To reach a high GCSE grade, weigh structural weaknesses against the decisions of powerful members and the impact of the Depression.

Structure

No permanent League army; decisions often required unanimity; sanctions depended on member cooperation.

Membership

The USA never joined; Germany and USSR were initially excluded, and Japan, Germany and Italy later left.

Self-interest of Britain and France

They hesitated to confront Japan and Italy, feared a costly war and valued their own economic and strategic interests.

Depression

Economic pressures made international sanctions and military commitments unattractive.

Manchuria, 1931–33

Delays and weak enforcement allowed a major member state to defy the Covenant.

Abyssinia, 1935–36

Ineffective sanctions, Suez and Hoare–Laval exposed political unwillingness to resist aggression.

Historians disagree: A. J. P. Taylor associated the decisive collapse with the Hoare–Laval revelations; other explanations stress the Depression, lack of US membership and flawed decision-making. Evaluate rather than memorise one “correct” cause.

How to write a 16-mark judgement

1. Establish a clear line of argument. 2. Explain at least two well-supported reasons, using specific events. 3. Test an alternative interpretation. 4. Judge which cause was most important and why, considering whether the League might have survived with different political choices.

SPaG: accurate spelling, punctuation and subject terminology can add 4 marks where indicated.
